# Manipulating the outcome of stable matching and roommates problems

**Abstract**

The stable marriage and stable roommates problems have been extensively studied due to their high applicability in various real-world scenarios. However, it might happen that no stable solution exists, or stable solutions do not meet certain requirements. In such cases, one might be interested in modifying the instance so that the existence of a stable outcome with the desired properties is ensured.

We focus on three different modifications. In stable roommates problems with all capacities being one, we give a simpler proof to show that removing an agent from each odd cycle of a stable partition is optimal. We further show that the problem becomes NP-complete if the capacities are greater than one, or the deleted agents must belong to a fixed subset of vertices.

Motivated by inverse optimization problems, we investigate how to modify the preferences of the agents as little as possible so that a given matching becomes stable. The deviation of the new preferences from the original ones can be measured in various ways; here we concentrate on the \(\ell_1\)-norm. We show that, assuming the Unique Games Conjecture, the problem does not admit a better than 2 approximation. By relying on bipartite-submodular functions, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for the bipartite case. We also show that a similar approach leads to a 2-approximation for general graphs.

Last, we consider problems where the preferences of agents are not fully prescribed, and the goal is to decide whether the preference lists can be extended so that a stable matching exists. We settle the complexity of several variants, including cases when some of the edges are required to be included or excluded from the solution.

**Keywords:** Inverse optimization, Preference extension, Stable matching, Stable roommates problem, Vertex deletion

### 1 Introduction

The stable marriage problem was introduced by Gale and Shapley in 1962 in their seminal paper [13]. Since then, an enormous amount of research has been done in the field; see for example [22] for a survey.

Our work belongs to the line of research that studies modifications of the preference system in order to get a stable solution with certain properties. Preference modifications in stable matching problems have been widely studied, mainly from a strategic point of view, where a given agent or a coalition of agents wants to submit false preferences in order to achieve better results. This setting is also closely related to inverse optimization problems, where we are given a feasible solution to an underlying optimization problem together with a linear weight function, and the goal is to modify the weights as little as possible so that the input solution becomes optimal; for further details on inverse optimization, see e.g. [10, 24].

## Previous work.

Concerning edge modifications, Abraham et al. [1] considered the problem of finding a matching in the roommates problem that has a minimum number of blocking edges. They showed that the problem is hard and is also hard to approximate. Biró et al. [4] studied a similar question for the marriage problem, where the goal is to find a maximum matching with minimum number of blocking edges. Tan [27] considered the problem of finding a maximum number of disjoint pairs of persons such that these pairs are stable among themselves, and gave an algorithm for determining an optimum solution.

Roth [25] showed that there is no matching mechanism that produces a stable matching and is strategy-proof for every agent, but the Gale-Shapley algorithm is at least strategy- proof for one side. Coalitional manipulations were studied by Shen et al. [26]. Hosseini et al. [17] investigated cases where the coalition can contain both men and women. Aziz et al. [3] investigated the case where the agents who want to manipulate the outcome have capacity larger than one, like firms or hospitals. Coalitional manipulations where a fixed subset of edges must be contained in the output of the Gale-Shapley algorithm has been studied by Kobayashi and Matsui [20] and by Gupta and Roy [15].

Modifying the preferences by ‘bribing’ the agents in order to have a stable matching satisfying certain conditions was studied by Boehmer et al. [5]. They examined several variants in terms of manipulative actions and manipulation goals in bipartite preference systems. Later, Eiben et al. [12] extended their work to the capacitated case. Finding a matching that is robust with respect to small modifications of the preferences have been studied by Chen et al. [7].

Stable matchings with forced and forbidden edges were considered by several papers, see Dias et al. [11], Cseh and Manlove [9], Cseh and Heeger [8].

## Our results.

One of the difficulties in markets that can be described as stable roommates problems is that they might not have a stable solution at all. To overcome this difficulty, a natural idea is to exclude certain agents or contracts from the market in order to guarantee the existence of a stable outcome. Both cases have been studied already, we concentrate on the deletion of agents. The latter problem was previously solved by Tan [27] who gave an algorithm based on Irving’s algorithm [18]. We give a significantly simpler approach to show that deleting an agent from each odd cycle in a stable partition is optimal. We also study the case when the cost of excluding someone might differ from agent to agent, or when only agents of some fixed subset are allowed to be removed, and show that these problems are NP-hard as well as when agents have nonnegative integer capacities.

In certain applications, it might happen that the central authority already has a most preferred outcome and it wants to make this outcome acceptable to the agents, too, by possibly compensating them. We concentrate on the problem where to goal is to bribe the agents in order to make a given outcome stable. We consider a more general framework than the one in [5] and [12]. In our framework, the preferences are given with real numbers, and instead of swap distance we work with the \(\ell_1\)-norm. This model allows to express that the differences between two adjacent agents in a preference list might differ a lot, whereas in swap distance<tbc>

interchanging any two of them would count as only one swap. In addition, this approach also makes possible to have ties among agents. We show that the problem is solvable in bipartite graphs in the capacitated setting, even when upper and lower bounds are given on the changes and the compensation cost differs for each agent. We also consider the roommate case which has not yet been investigated before. We show that the problem is NP-hard, but it admits a 2-approximation.

Finally, we investigate problems where the preferences are manipulated by the agents themselves in order to force or avoid certain contracts to form. While previous papers only considered manipulations with respect to the outcome of the Gale-Shapley algorithm, we investigate more general cases. Our goal is to ensure that there exists a stable matching with respect to the modified preferences. This can be practically important, for example when a stable matching is chosen randomly, not by the Gale-Shapley algorithm. We also study cases where there are forbidden edges instead of forced ones, or some places in the preferences are fixed and cannot be manipulated. We show that almost all problems arising this way are NP-complete even in rather restricted settings. On the positive side, we give an algorithm for the case when certain places in the preference lists are not allowed to be manipulated by the agents.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Basic notation and definitions are introduced in Section 2. Section 3 focuses on problems where the goal is to ensure the existence of a stable matching through the deletion of a subset of vertices. Preference modifications in order to make a given outcome stable are discussed in Section 4. Finally, in Section 5, we investigate preference extension problems.

## 2 Preliminaries

## Submodular and bipartite-submodular set functions.

A set function \(f:2^V\rightarrow R\) is called _submodular_ if \(f(X)+f(Y)\ge f(X\cup Y)+f(X\cap Y)\) holds for every \(X,Y\subseteq V\) . It is known that this is equivalent to \(f(X+a)+f(X+b)\ge f(X+a+b)+f(X)\) for every \(X\subseteq V\) and distinct \(a,b\in V\backslash X\). A function _f_ defined on the vertex set of a bipartite graph _G_=(_A,B;E_) is _bipartite-submodular_ if there exist two submodular functions _f<sub>A</sub>_ and _f<sub>B</sub>_ defined on _A_ and _B_, respectively, such that \(f(X)=f_A(X\cap A)+f_B(X\cap B)\) for every \(X\subseteq A\cup B\). The following result appeared in \[16\].

**Theorem 1** (Hochbaum)**.** _Given a bipartite graph G_=(_A,B;E_) _and a polynomial-time computable submodular cost function_ \(c:2^{A\cup B}\rightarrow E\)_, the minimum cost vertex cover problem can be 2-approximated in polynomial time. Furthermore, if c is also bipartite-submodular, then a minimum cost vertex cover can be found in polynomial time._

## Stable matchings.

Let _G_=(_V,E_) be an undirected simple graph, and let _\<<sub>u</sub>_ be a linear order on _N(u_) for each \(u\in V\) . The pair (_G,\>_) is called a _stable roommates instance_. If _G_ is bipartite, then (_G,\>_) is a _stable marriage instance_. If ties are allowed, i.e., _\<<sub>u</sub>_ are weak orders, then (_G,\>_) is a _stable roommates instance with ties_. For a stable roommates instance (_G_=(_V,E),\>_) and a matching \(M\subseteq E\), an edge \(uv\in E\backslash M\) is _blocking_ if _u_ prefers _v_ to its partner in _M_ (or has no partner in _M_) and _v_ prefers _u_ to its partner in _M_ (or has no partner in _M_). If no blocking edge exists, then _M_ is a _stable matching_.

Let (_G,\>_) be a stable roommates instance. A _stable partition of_ (_G,\>_) is a permutation \(\pi:V\rightarrow V\) such that for each \(u\in V\) , (i) if \(\pi(u)\neq\pi^{-1}(u)\), then \(u\pi(u),u\pi^{-1}(u)\in E\) and \(\pi(u)>_u\pi^{-1}(u)\), and (ii) for each _v_ adjacent to _u_, if \(\pi(u)=u\) or \(v>_u\pi^{-1}(u)\), then \(\pi^{-1}(v)>_vu\). The cycles of the permutation \(\pi\) partition the agents into _odd_ and _even cycles_ depending on the parity of their lengths. We call an agent _u_ a _singleton in_ \(\pi\) if \(\pi(u)=u\). The following fundamental result is due to Tan \[28\].

**Theorem 2** (Tan)**.** _Any stable roommates instance_ (_G,\>_) _admits a stable partition_ \(\pi\)_, and such a partition can be found in_ O(|_V_|<sup>2</sup>) _time. Furthermore, each stable partition has the same set of singleton agents and the same set of odd cycles. There exists a stable matching if and only if there exist a stable partition without odd cycles of length_ \(\ge 3\).

We will also need the notion of weak stability. Let (_G_=(_V,E),\>_) be a stable roommates instance with ties, and let \(M\subseteq E\) be a matching. An edge \(uv\in E\backslash M\) _strongly blocks M_ if _u_ strictly prefers _v_ to its partner in _M_ (or has no partner in _M_) and _v_ strictly prefers _u_ to its partner in _M_ (or has no partner in _M_). If no strongly blocking edge exists, then _M_ is a _weakly stable matching_.

We also consider cases where the vertices of _G_ have nonnegative integer capacities _q(v_). In such an instance, we call \(M\subseteq E\) a _q-matching_ if \(|M(v)|\le q(v)\) for each \(v\in V\) . A vertex is _unsaturated_ in _M_ if |_M(v_)|_\<q(v_). We say that an edge \(uv\in E\backslash M\) _blocks M_ if both _u_ and _v_ are either unsaturated by _M_ or strictly prefer the other to some of their partners in _M_. The _q_-matching _M_ is called a _stable q-matching_ if it is not blocked by any edge. We also say that an edge \(uv\in E\backslash M\) is _dominated_ at _u_ if |_M(u_)|=_q(u_) and for all \(xu\in M(u)\), we have _x\><sub>u</sub>v_. Clearly a _q_-matching _M_ is stable if and only if each \(uv\in E\backslash M\) is dominated at either _u_ or _v_.

The hardness of the following problem, proved by Manlove et al. \[23\], is a useful tool for proving NP-completeness of various stable matching problems.

The following two versions of the stable marriage with ties problem was proven to be NP- complete by Cseh and Heeger \[8\].

A _one-sided preference model_ involves a bipartite graph _G_=(_A,B;E_) and linear orders _\><sub>a</sub>_ on _N(a_) for every \(a\in A\). A matching _M_ is _Pareto-optimal_ if there is no matching \(M'\) that is better than _M_ for some agent in _A_, and at least as good as _M_ for the other agents in _A_. Some hardness proofs in Section 5 will be based on the following NP-complete problem, introduced by Abraham et al. \[2\].

Given a bipartite graph _G_=(_A,B;E_) with preferences for each \(a\in A\) and a matching _M_, a _coalition_ is a cycle (_a_<sub>1</sub>_,b_<sub>1</sub>_,a_<sub>2</sub>_,...,b<sub>r</sub>_), such that \(a_ib_i\in M\) for each \(i\in[r]\) and each agent prefers _b_<sub>_i_+1</sub> to _b<sub>i</sub>_. The matching is _non-wasteful_ if there is no element of _B_ that is not covered by _M_, but is preferred by an agent in _A_ to his current partner. Abraham et al. verified the following.

**Theorem 3** (Abraham et al.)**.** _A matching M (in the one sided preference model) is Pareto- optimal if and only if it is maximal, non-wasteful, and coalition-free._

## 3 Vertex deletion

In this section, we study the problem of removing vertices so that the remaining graph has a stable matching. Two variants are considered: in the first one, the aim is to remove the minimum number of vertices, while in the second one, an arbitrary number of vertices can be removed, but only from a given vertex subset \(T\subseteq V\) .

Let _G_=(_V,E_) be a graph with strict preferences _\><sub>v</sub>_ for each vertex \(v\in V\) . A vertex set \(S\subseteq V\) is _removable_ if _G-S_ admits a stable matching. When vertex capacities _q(v_) are considered, a vertex set \(S\subseteq V\) is _removable_ if _G-S_ admits a stable _q_-matching.

The analogous edge-deletion problems are also of interest, and have already been studied in the literature. The minimization version is equivalent to finding a matching that has the smallest possible number of blocking pairs. This problem was shown to be NP-hard by Abraham et al. \[1\], even for complete preference lists. The subset version is equivalent to the following: given an edge subset \(F\subseteq E\), is there a matching in _G_ for which every blocking edge is in _F_? This problem is called _stable roommates with free edges_, and was shown to be NP-complete by Cechlárová and Fleiner \[6\].

Among the vertex deletion problems, vertex-del-sr was considered by Tan \[27\] who gave an algorithm based on Irving’s algorithm \[18\]. In the following, we give a significantly simpler algorithm for vertex-del-sr. We also show that vertex-subset-del-sr is NP-complete. The latter implies that finding a minimum weight removable set is NP-complete even for vertex weights in {0,1}, and it is inapproximable, since it is hard to decide if there is a removable set of weight 0.

We show that it is very easy to determine a minimum cardinality removable vertex set using a stable partition. The algorithm is presented as Algorithm 1; it chooses an arbitrary vertex from each odd cycle in the stable partition. Note, however, that a removable set does not necessarily contain a vertex from each odd cycle, so optimality is not obvious. We show the correctness of the algorithm in the proof of the theorem below.

It remains to show that the size of a removable set cannot be smaller than the number of odd cycles in a stable partition.

**Claim 6.** _The minimum size of a removable set is equal to the number of odd cycles of length at least_ 3 _in any stable partition_ \(\pi\).

_Proof._ Let _S_<sup>∗</sup> be a removable set, and let _M_<sup>∗</sup> be a stable matching in _G-S_<sup>∗</sup>. Since \(\pi\) is a stable partition, every odd cycle of length at least 3 in \(\pi\) must either have a vertex in _S_<sup>∗</sup> or a vertex _u_ matched in _M_<sup>∗</sup> to a partner better than \(\pi^{-1}(u)\). Indeed, if this does not hold for a cycle, then there is a vertex _v_ in the cycle that is unmatched or matched to a worse partner than \(v\pi(v)\) and \(v\pi^{-1}(v)\). But then \(\pi^{-1}(v)v\) blocks, since \(\pi^{-1}(v)\) is not matched to anyone that is better than _v_ by our assumption. We call a vertex \(v\in V\backslash S^*\) _out-dominated_ if it is matched in _M_<sup>∗</sup> to a vertex \(u\neq\pi(v)\) with \(u>_v\pi^{-1}(v)\). A vertex _u_ is an _in-dominator_ if it is the partner in _M_<sup>∗</sup> of an out-dominated vertex _v_. Note that _u_ prefers \(\pi(u)\) and \(\pi^{-1}(u)\) to _v_ because \(\pi\) is a stable partition.

Let _C_={_v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>t</sub>_} be an arbitrary cycle of length at least 2 in \(\pi\) such that \(\pi(v_i)=v_{i+1}\), and let _v_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,v<sub>i<sub>z</sub></sub>_ be the in-dominator vertices in _C_. Observe that these vertices are pairwise non-adjacent on the cycle _C_ as an adjacent pair would block _M_<sup>∗</sup>. Also, each of _v_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub>-1</sub>_,...,v_<sub>_i<sub>z</sub>_-1</sub> must be either in _S_<sup>∗</sup> or out-dominated. Indeed, if for some \(1\le j\le z\) the vertex _v_<sub>_i<sub>j</sub>_-1</sub> is not in _S_<sup>∗</sup> and also not out-dominated, then the edge _v_<sub>_i<sub>j</sub>_-1</sub>_v<sub>i<sub>j</sub></sub>_ blocks as _v<sub>i<sub>j</sub></sub>_ is an in-dominator.

Suppose now that _t_ is odd. We claim that there is at least one vertex in _C_\\{_v_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub>-1</sub>_,...,v_<sub>_i<sub>z</sub>_-1</sub>} that is either in _S_<sup>∗</sup> or is out-dominated. To see this, consider the paths obtained by removing the vertices {_v_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub>-1</sub>_,v_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,v_<sub>_i<sub>z</sub>_-1</sub>_,v<sub>i<sub>z</sub></sub>_} from _C_. Since _t_ is odd, one of the paths contains an odd number of vertices; we may assume that this path is _v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>p</sub>_ for some odd _p_. If none of these vertices is deleted or out-dominated, then at least one them, say _v<sub>i</sub>_, must be unmatched or matched in _M_<sup>∗</sup> to a vertex worse than \(\pi^{-1}(v_i)\). If \(i\neq 1\), then _v_<sub>_i_-1</sub>_v<sub>i</sub>_ blocks _M_<sup>∗</sup>, a contradiction. If _i_=1, then \(v_t=\pi^{-1}(v_1)\) is an in-dominator as _v_<sub>1</sub> is the first vertex of the path. This implies<tbc>

that _v<sub>t</sub>v_<sub>1</sub> blocks _M_<sup>∗</sup>, a contradiction again. That is, at least one of the vertices _v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>p</sub>_ is deleted or out-dominated.

We conclude that the number of in-dominators in each odd cycle _C_ is at most the sum of the numbers of out-dominated and deleted vertices in _C_ minus one. If _C_ is an even cycle, then the number of in-dominators is at most the sum of the numbers of out-dominated and deleted vertices. Finally, a singleton in \(\pi\) cannot be an in-dominator. It follows from the definitions that the number of in-dominators and the number of out-dominated vertices are the same. By combining these observations, we get that |_S_<sup>∗</sup>| is at least the number of odd cycles in \(\pi\).

The theorem follows by Claims 5 and 6.

We now show that the subset version of the problem is hard.

**Theorem 7.** vertex-subset-del-sr _is NP-complete._

_Proof._ The problem is clearly in NP. To show hardness, we reduce from com-smti, see the definition in Section 2.

Consider an instance (_G_=(_A,B;E),\>_) of com-smti, where _A_={_a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>n</sub>_}, _B_={_b_<sub>1</sub>_,...,b<sub>n</sub>_}, and ties are restricted to a subset \(b_1,\dots,b_\ell\), each of which have two neighbors. We create an instance of vertex-subset-del-sr as follows, see Figure 1b for an example. For each \(a_i\in A\), we add three agents \(a'_i\), _x<sub>i</sub>_ and \(x'_i\). For each \(i\in[\ell]\), we add three agents \(b'_i\), \(b''_i\) and _y<sub>i</sub>_. Finally, for \(i=\ell+1,\dots,n\), we add an agent \(b'_i\). ## 4 Preference modifications

In this section, we consider problems where the goal is to make a given matching stable by bribing the agents to change their preferences. Each agent _v_ assigns a nonnegative real number _p<sub>v</sub>(u_) to each acceptable partner _u_. By abuse of notation, we extend this notation to edges incident to _v_ by setting _p<sub>v</sub>(uv_):=_p<sub>v</sub>(u_), and call this the _value_ of the edge _uv_ for _v_. The weak preference list of _v_ is derived from these values by declaring \(u\ge_vu'\) if and only if \(p_v(u)\ge p_v(u')\). The agents might also have positive integer capacities, denoted by _q(v_) for agent _v_.

The cost of modifying the preferences can be measured in various ways; here, we concentrate on the case of \(\ell_1\)-norm. That is, changing the value of _p<sub>v</sub>(u_) from _a_ to _b_ has cost |_a-b_|. If \(p'\) denotes the modified preference values, then the _cost of_ \(p'\) _(with respect to p)_ is \(\text{cost}(p'):=\sum_{v\in V}\sum_{u\in N(v)}|p_v(u)-p'_v(u)|\). The goal is to find a new preference matrix \(p'\) of minimum cost such that a given b-matching _M_ becomes weakly stable with respect to \(p'\).

First we show that the problem is not only NP-hard in general, but it is also hard to approximate within a factor better than 2.

**Theorem 12.** \(\ell_1\)-min-pm _is NP-hard even if each capacity is one. Furthermore, assuming the Unique Games Conjecture, it cannot be approximated within a factor of_ \(2-\varepsilon\) _for any_ \(\varepsilon>0\).

_Proof._ Observe that if each capacity is 1, then there always exists an optimal solution that changes the values only on the edges of _M_. Indeed, lowering the value of a non-matching edge _uv_ to become dominated at vertex _v_ has the same cost as increasing the value of the edge in _M(v_) for _v_ to dominate _uv_. By doing the latter, we are surely better off as other edges may become dominated too at _v_, while in the first case we do not make any progress on dominating the other edges.

The problem is clearly in NP. To show NP-hardness, we reduce from vertex-cover. Let _G_=(_V,E_) be an instance of the minimum vertex cover problem. We construct an instance \((G'=(V',E'),p,M)\) of \(\ell_1\)-min-pm. Let \(V'=\{v',v''|v\in V\}\) and \(E'=\{u'v'|uv\in E\}\cup\{v'v''|v\in V\}\). Furthermore, set \(M=\{v'v''|v\in V\}\). For each vertex \(v\in V\) , we define \(p_{v^\prime}(v'')=p_{v^{\prime\prime}}(v')=0\) and set all the other \(p_{v^\prime}(u')\) values to be 1, see Figure 2.

Let \(p'\) be a minimum cost solution of the \(\ell_1\)-min-pm instance thus obtained. By the observation above, we may assume that \(p'\) differs from _p_ only on edges of _M_. Since vertices in \(\{v''|v\in V\}\) are matched with their only partner, their preference values do not change. Clearly, for each vertex \(v'\), we have either \(p'_{v^\prime}(v'')=0\) or \(p'_{v^\prime}(v'')=1\). Furthermore, at least one of the end vertices of each original edge increases the value of the incident matching edge to 1, hence the set of such vertices forms a vertex cover. Vice versa, if we increase the values of the matching edges on the vertices of a vertex cover, then no original edge of _G_ blocks _M_.

By the above, minimum vertex cover in _G_ is equivalent to \(\ell_1\)-min-pm in \((G',p,M)\), concluding the proof of NP-hardness. Assuming the Unique Games Conjecture, vertex-cover cannot be approximated within a factor better than 2 by a result of Khoth and Regev \[19\], implying the second half of the theorem.

As a positive result, we show that \(\ell_1\)-min-pm is polynomial-time solvable in bipartite graphs. Interestingly, our solution relies on Hochbaum’s algorithm for the minimum cost vertex cover problem under bipartite-submodular functions.

By the nonnegativity of _c_ and the fact that each vertex has degree one in _H_, there exists an optimal vertex cover that covers exactly one endpoint of each edge. Such a vertex cover has the same cost as dominating each edge at the chosen endpoint in an optimal way. This implies that the cost of an optimum vertex cover is equal to the cost of an optimal preference modification in the original \(\ell_1\)-min-pm instance. Furthermore, given an optimal vertex cover, the optimal modified preference values can be determined by solving the corresponding LPs, concluding the proof of the theorem.

The same reduction can be applied even if the original graph is not bipartite. However, then it is not possible to put each copy of a vertex on the same side of the auxiliary graph _H_ (which is a perfect matching), therefore the cost function \(c=\sum f_v\) cannot be written as the sum of two submodular cost functions, which means that, though it is submodular, it is not bipartite-submodular. Therefore, by Theorem 1, we get the following.

**Theorem 15.** _There is a polynomial-time 2-approximation algorithm for the_ \(\ell_1\)-min-pm _problem._

Note that, assuming the Unique Games Conjecture, the approximation given by Theorem 15 is best possible by Theorem 12. **Remark 16.** If an arbitrary (not necessarily maximal) _q_-matching _M_ is given and the goal is to modify the preferences in such a way that there exists a stable _q_-matching containing _M_, then the problem becomes difficult. ## 5 Preference extension problems

### 5.1 Fixed and arbitrary preferences

Now we turn our attention to problems where the preference list of each agent is either fixed or can be set arbitrarily. Such problems may arise, for example, when dealing with cheating strategies, where some of the agents might submit falsified preferences in order to get a desired stable matching.

Similar problems have been considered before, see e.g. \[15, 20\]. Kobayashi et al. \[20\] investigated problems where each preference list has to be complete. They showed that if the preferences are fixed for each man, then deciding whether there are preference lists of the women such that a partial matching _M_ is included in the men-optimal stable matching is NP-complete. On the positive side, they showed that if the preferences of all the women unmatched by _M_ are fixed too, then the problem becomes polynomial-time solvable.

The problems that we consider differ from previous results in several aspects: the completeness of the preference lists is not always assumed, the underlying graph might be non-bipartite, and some of the edges might be forced or forbidden to be contained in a stable matching. It should be emphasized that we are interested not only in men-optimal stable matchings, but in the existence of a stable matching satisfying the constraints in general.

The problems that are featured in this section are the followings.

**Question:** Are there preferences for the rest of the women such that there exists a stable matching containing \(\mu\)?

## 5.2 Fixed entries in the preference lists

We move on to problems where the preference lists of the agents have some fixed places that cannot be modified. The setting we concentrate on is the following. We are given a graph _G_=(_V,E_) with vertex capacities _q(v_) for \(v\in V\) and an inclusionwise maximal feasible _q_- matching \(M\subseteq E\). For a saturated vertex _v_ and edge \(e\in M(v)\), we have a fixed number _p<sub>v</sub>(e_) denoting that _e_ is the _p<sub>v</sub>(e_)-th worst edge in _v_’s ranking on the incident edges. Furthermore, a similar _p<sub>v</sub>(e_) value might be given for other vertex-edge pairs as well. Note that the _p<sub>v</sub>(e_) values for \(e\in M(v)\) where _v_ is non-saturated are not interesting in the sense that no edge can be dominated at such a vertex. The task is to determine whether there exists an extension of these partial preference lists such that the given _q_-matching _M_ is stable. Such an extension is called a _stable preference extension_. In a sense, this problem is the inverse of the stable _q_-matching problem, where the preferences are set in advance and the task is to find a stable _q_-matching _M_.

INC-MAX-SPE

Input: A graph _G_=(_V,E_), vertex capacities \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_+^V\), an inclusionwise maximal feasible _q_-matching \(M\subseteq E\), preference values _p<sub>v</sub>(e_) for each saturated vertex \(v\in V\) and \(e\in M(v)\), and preference values for some other vertex-edge pairs.

Question: Does there exist a preference extension for which _M_ is stable?

We show that the problem of finding a stable preference extension can be reduced to computing a maximum stable matching in a bipartite graph.

**Theorem 29.** _For any graph G_=(_V,E), q-matching M and partial preference p which fixes p<sub>v</sub>(e_) _for each saturated vertex v and each edge_ \(e\in M\) _containing v,_ inc-max-spe _an be solved in polynomial time._

_Proof._ We reduce the problem to deciding if there exists a matching that covers a given side of a bipartite graph _H_=(_U,W;F_) entirely. We may assume that there is no edge \(e\in E\backslash M\) whose rank is fixed on both of its vertices in such a way that _e_ necessarily blocks _M_, as otherwise the answer is clearly ‘NO’. Also, we may assume that no edge \(e\in E\backslash M\) has a fixed rank at a vertex where all edges in _M_ have better rank, because then _e_ is dominated and can be removed.

We construct a bipartite graph _H_=(_U,W;F_) as follows. For each saturated vertex \(v\in V\) , we add vertices _v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v_<sub>_p<sub>v</sub>(f_)-1</sub> to _U_ where _f_ is the worst edge for _v_ in _M_. If _p<sub>v</sub>(f_)=1, then we do not include any copies of _v_. Also, if there is an index \(1\le j\le p_v(f)-1\) such that _j_ is already assigned to an edge, then we delete that copy of _v_ from the graph. For each edge \(e\notin M\) we add a vertex _v<sub>e</sub>_ to _W_. Finally, we add an edge between a copy _v<sub>j</sub>_ of a vertex \(v\in V\) and a vertex _v<sub>e</sub>_ corresponding to edge \(e\in E(v)\) if and only if _p<sub>v</sub>(e_) is not yet fixed.

We claim that the preferences can be extended in such a way that _M_ is a stable _q_-matching if and only if _H_ admits a matching covering the vertices in _W_. First suppose there is a matching _N_ in _H_ covering all vertices in _W_. We allocate the unassigned preferences of the saturated vertices that are worse than its worst edge in any order to the edges that are matched to its copies in _N_. The remaining preferences are chosen arbitrarily from the free positions. Then _M_ will become a stable _q_-matching of _G_ with respect to those preferences, since any edge contains a vertex that is saturated with strictly better edges.

For the other direction, suppose that it is possible to extend the preferences in _G_ such that _M_ becomes stable. If we take the matching _M_ in _H_ that matches _v<sub>j</sub>_ to the vertex corresponding to its _j_’th worst edge, then _M_ covers all vertices in _W_ as an uncovered vertex would correspond to a blocking edge.

As a matching covering the vertices in _W_ can be found in polynomial time, the theorem follows.

As a slightly more general problem, suppose that lower and upper bounds \(\ell_v(e)\) and _u<sub>v</sub>(e_) are given for each vertex \(v\in V\) and edge incident to _v_. The goal is to extend the preferences in such a way that _M_ is stable and \(\ell_v(e)\le p_v(e)\le u_v(e)\) holds for each vertex _v_ and each edge _e_ adjacent to _v_.

**Theorem 30.** _If only lower bounds are given, then_ inc-max-SPE _can be solved in polynomial time._

_Proof._ We give an algorithm consisting of four phases.

_Phase 1:_ We construct a bipartite graph _H_=(_U,W;F_) similarly as in the proof of the unbounded case (Theorem 29). For each saturated vertex \(u\in V\) , we add _p<sub>u</sub>(f_)-_k<sub>u</sub>_ copies of _u_ to _U_, where _f_ is the worst edge for _u_ in _M_ and _k<sub>u</sub>_ is the number of fixed values in the first _p<sub>u</sub>(f_) places. Also, for each edge \(e\in E\backslash M\) that is not dominated already, we add a vertex _v<sub>e</sub>_ to _W_. We add an edge between a copy _u<sub>j</sub>_ of a vertex \(u\in V\) and a vertex _v<sub>e</sub>_ corresponding to an edge \(e\in E(u)\) if and only if _p<sub>u</sub>(e_) is not yet fixed and \(j\ge\ell_u(e)\).

We check whether there exists a matching that covers all vertices of _W_; such a matching corresponds to the domination of the edges in _E_\\_M_ not yet dominated. If no such matching exists, then the algorithm stops with the answer ‘NO’, the preferences cannot be extended in such a way that _M_ is a stable _q_-matching and the lower bounds are met. Otherwise, let _N_<sub>1</sub> be a matching covering _W_.

_Phase 2:_ We extend the bipartite graph _H_ by adding another vertex to _W_ for each edge that was not dominated originally, and two vertices for every edge that was not considered in Phase 1. That is, for each edge \(e=xy\in E\), there are two corresponding vertices \(v_e^x\) and \(v_e^y\) in _W_. We modify the edges of _H_ in such a way that \(v_e^x\) is only connected to the copies _x<sub>i</sub>_ of _x_ and \(v_e^y\) is only connected to the copies _y<sub>j</sub>_ of _y_ where \(i\ge\ell_x(e)\) an \(j\ge\ell_y(e)\), respectively. Finally,<tbc>

<tbc>we construct a matching _N_<sub>2</sub> in the extended bipartite graph by adding \(v_e^uu_j\) to _N_<sub>2</sub> for each \(v_eu_j\in N_1\).

_Phase 3:_ Starting from the matching _N_<sub>2</sub>, we check whether there exists a matching that covers all vertices of _U_ using the Hungarian method \[21\]. If no such matching exists, then the preferences cannot be extended in such a way that _M_ is a stable _q_-matching and the lower bounds are met, and the algorithm stops with the answer ‘NO’. If there exists such a matching, then a nice feature of the algorithm is that once a vertex becomes covered, it remains so throughout. Hence, for each edge _e=xy_, one of the vertices \(v_e^x\) and \(v_e^y\) is covered. We denote the resulting matching by _N_<sub>3</sub>.

_Phase 4:_ We further extend _H_ by adding all the copies of each vertex \(u\in V\) to _U_ that have not been added in Phase 1. Also, we extend the set of edges such that there is an edge \(u_jv_e^u\) for each \(u\in V\) , \(e\in E(u)\backslash M(u)\) and \(j\ge\ell_u(e)\). Consider the vertices corresponding to edges _e_ that were isolated until the addition of the new edges, that is, satisfied \(\ell_u(e)\ge min\{p_u(f)|f\in M(u)\}\). We check if these vertices can all be matched to vertices not covered by _N_<sub>3</sub> by running the Hungarian algorithm. If no such matching exists, then there is no preference extension satisfying the lower bounds at all, and the algorithm outputs ‘NO’.

Otherwise, let _N_<sub>4</sub> denote the matching obtained. We claim that the matching \(N_3\cup N_4\) can be extended to a matching in such a way that it covers all vertices in _H_. To see this, observe that only lower bounds are given and for each remaining copy \(v_e^u\) of an edge, the lower bound \(\ell_u(e)\) is smaller than the indices of the uncovered copies of _u_. Indeed, all \(v_e^u\) vertices with \(l_u(e)\ge min\{p_u(f)|f\in M(u)\}\) are matched by _N_<sub>4</sub>, and for each \(u\in V\) the copies _u<sub>j</sub>_ with \(j\le min\{p_u(f)|f\in M(u)\}\) are matched by _N_<sub>3</sub>. Therefore, the graph induced by the unmatched vertices consists of a union of complete bipartite graphs with equal sized color classes, so it admits a perfect matching _N_<sub>5</sub>.

Setting the preferences according to \(N_3\cup N_4\cup N_5\) gives a preference extension that satisfies all conditions.

**Remark 31.** Theorems 29 and 30 can be straightforwardly extended to hypergraphs. That is, given a hypergraph _H_=(_V,_E), vertex capacities \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_+^V\), a feasible _q_-matching \(M\subseteq\mathcal{E}\), preference values _p<sub>v</sub>(f_) for \(v\in V\) and \(f\in M(v)\), preference values for some other vertex- hyperedge pairs, and lower bounds \(\ell_v(f)\) for \(v\in V\) , \(f\in E(v)\), one can decide in polynomial time if there exists a preference extension for which _M_ is stable.

A further extension would be to consider _q_-matchings _M_ that are not necessarily inclusion- wise maximal. Let _M_ be an arbitrary _q_-matching and suppose that the places in the preference lists of the agents are fixed for the edges of _M_ for each saturated vertex and maybe on some other vertex-edge pairs, too. The goal is to set the remaining preferences in such a way that there exists a stable _q_-matching \(M'\) containing _M_.

Forced-SPE

**Input:** A graph _G_=(_V,E_), vertex capacities \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_+^V\), a feasible _q_-matching \(\mu\subseteq E\), preference values _p<sub>v</sub>(e_) for each saturated vertex \(v\in V\) and \(e\in\mu(v)\), and preference values for some other vertex-edge pairs.

**Question:** Does there exist a preference extension together with a stable _q_-matching _M_ for which \(\mu\subseteq M\)?

Surprisingly, this problem becomes NP-complete even for the stable marriage case.

**Theorem 32.** forced-spe _is NP complete even for bipartite graphs with capacity one on each vertex._

_Proof._ The problem is clearly in NP. To show NP-hardness, we reduce from x3c, see the definition in Section 2.

Let _I_ be an instance of x3c. We construct an instance \(I'\) with _H_=(_U,W;F_) of forced- spe as follows. Let _P_={_p_<sub>1</sub>_,...,p_<sub>3_n_</sub>} be a set of agents corresponding to the ground set _S_, and _Q_={_q_<sub>1</sub>_,...,q<sub>m</sub>_} be a set of agents corresponding to the 3-sets. These two sets of agents form one color class of the bipartite graph which will be referred to as men. Agents in _X_={_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>m</sub>_}, _Y_={_y_<sub>1</sub>_,...,y<sub>m</sub>_} and _Z_={_z_<sub>1</sub>_,...,z_<sub>3_n_</sub>} form the other color class of the bipartite graph which will be referred to as women. Finally, we add a special agent _u_ to the set of men and a special agent _w_ to the set of women. So \(U=P\cup Q\cup\{u\}\), \(W=X\cup Y\cup Z\cup\{w\}\).

The forced matching is \(\mu=\{uw,p_iz_i|i\in[3n]\}\). The fixed preferences of the agents on the edges of \(\mu\) are the following:

• for _u_, the rank of _M(u_) is _m-n_+1,<tbc>

• for a man _p<sub>i</sub>_, the rank of _M(p<sub>i</sub>_) is 2,<tbc>

• for a woman _z<sub>i</sub>_, the rank of _M(z<sub>i</sub>_) is set arbitrarily.

We further add the edges \(\{ux_i,x_iq_i,q_iy_i|i\in[m]\}\) to _F_, and for each 3-set _C<sub>j</sub>_={_s_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,s_<sub>_i_<sub>2</sub></sub>_,s_<sub>_i_<sub>3</sub></sub>} of _I_ we add the edges _y<sub>j</sub>p_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub></sub>, _y<sub>j</sub>p_<sub>_i_<sub>2</sub></sub> and _y<sub>j</sub>p_<sub>_i_<sub>3</sub></sub>.

We claim that there is an exact 3-cover in _I_ if and only if the preferences can be extended in a way that there is a stable matching _M_ containing \(\mu\). Let us first suppose that _C_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,C<sub>i<sub>n</sub></sub>_ is a solution of the x3c instance _I_. Let _M_ be the matching obtained by adding the edges \(\{x_{i_j}q_{i_j}|j\in[n]\}\) and the edges \(\{q_ky_k|k\notin\{i_1,\dots,i_n\}\}\) to \(\mu\). The preferences are set such that the _m-n_ places worse than that of _uw_ for _u_ are given to the edges \(\{ux_k|k\notin\{i_1,\dots,i_n\}\}\). For \(k\notin\{i_1,\dots,i_n\}\), we set _q<sub>k</sub>_ to prefer _y<sub>k</sub>_ to _x<sub>k</sub>_. For \(j\in[n]\), we set _q<sub>i<sub>j</sub></sub>_ to prefer _x<sub>i<sub>j</sub></sub>_ to _y<sub>i<sub>j</sub></sub>_ and _x<sub>i<sub>j</sub></sub>_ to prefer _q<sub>i<sub>j</sub></sub>_ to _u_. Also for each _i_=1_,..._3_n_, we set the worst position of _p<sub>i</sub>_ to be the _y<sub>j</sub>_ corresponding to the set \(C_j\in\{C_{i_1},\dots C_{i_n}\}\) containing the element _a<sub>i</sub>_. Since _C_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,C<sub>i<sub>n</sub></sub>_ is a partition, there is no collision when doing this. Then, all edges not in _M_ are dominated: each edge of type _ux<sub>j</sub>_ is dominated at either _u_ or _x<sub>j</sub>_, each edge \(q_jx_j\notin M\) is dominated at _q<sub>j</sub>_, each edge \(q_jy_j\notin M\) is dominated at _q<sub>j</sub>_, and each edge _p<sub>i</sub>y<sub>j</sub>_ is dominated at either _y<sub>j</sub>_ or _p<sub>i</sub>_.

For the other direction, suppose there is a preference extension and a matching _M_ with \(\mu\subseteq M\) that satisfy the conditions. For any triple _x<sub>i</sub>_, _q<sub>i</sub>_, and _y<sub>i</sub>_, one of these vertices must be uncovered in _M_ since the only possible partner of both _x<sub>i</sub>_ and _y<sub>i</sub>_ is _q<sub>i</sub>_ as the other neighbors are already matched in \(\mu\). There are _m-n_ women _x<sub>i</sub>_ such that _x<sub>i</sub>_ is worse for _u_ than _w_. At the same time, there must be _n_ women _x_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,x<sub>i<sub>n</sub></sub>_ that are better, so for the edges _ux<sub>i<sub>j</sub></sub>_ to be dominated we must have \(x_{i_j}q_{i_j}\in M'\). Then _y<sub>i<sub>j</sub></sub>_ cannot be matched for _j_=1_,...n_, hence the edges that join these vertices to _P_ must be dominated at the vertices of _P_. But there are at least _n_ such _y<sub>i<sub>j</sub></sub>_-s with altogether 3_n_ edges incident to them and each \(p_i\in P\) can dominate at most one such edge, therefore _C_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,C<sub>i<sub>n</sub></sub>_ is necessarily a partition. \(\square\)

**Remark 33.** If the size of the maximal matching _M_ containing \(\mu\) is larger than the size of \(\mu\) only by a constant, then the problem can be solved in polynomial time.

**Remark 34.** The proof of Theorem 32 implies that the bipartite variant of forced-spe when the preferences are set on _M_ only for one class of the agents is also NP-complete.

**Remark 35.** If the graph is a complete bipartite graph, or a complete graph and the preferences are only set on the edges of \(\mu\), then the problem can be solved in polynomial time. First, check whether the edges that connect vertices matched by \(\mu\) can all be dominated as we did before. If this is possible, then find a perfect matching _M_ containing \(\mu\) and set the edges of \(M\backslash\mu\) as the best edges for every agent. Then _M_ is clearly a stable matching.

Now suppose that a set \(\tau\) of forbidden edges is given instead of forced ones while some preferences of the agents are fixed. The question is whether the preference lists can be extended such that there exists a stable matching _M_ disjoint from \(\tau\).

Interestingly, forbidden-spe turns out to be NP-hard even if there are no predefined preferences, each capacity is one and the graph is bipartite. In that case the problem is equivalent to the following: Given a bipartite graph _G_=(_A,B;E_) where _E_ is partitioned into red edges _E<sub>r</sub>_ and blue edges _E<sub>b</sub>_, decide if there is a matching _M_ in the subgraph _G<sub>r</sub>_=(_A,B;E<sub>r</sub>_) such that the vertices of _M_ cover every blue edge. We call this problem red-blue-edge-cover.

**Theorem 36.** red-blue-edge-cover _is NP-complete._

_Proof._ The problem is clearly in NP. To show NP-hardness, we reduce from 3sat.

Let \(\Phi\) be a 3sat instance with clauses _C_<sub>1</sub>_,...,C<sub>m</sub>_ and variables _x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>n</sub>_. We construct a bipartite graph _G_=(_A,B;E_) as follows. For each clause _C<sub>j</sub>_, we add two vertices \(c'_j\) and \(c''_j\) to _A_. For each literal _x<sub>i</sub>_ or \(\overline{x_i}\in C_j\), we add a vertex \(y_j^i\) or \(z_j^i\), respectively, to _B_. We connect these five vertices with red edges, that is, a red _K_<sub>2,3</sub> subgraph is added for every clause. For each variable _x<sub>i</sub>_, we add two vertices _y<sub>i</sub>_ and _z<sub>i</sub>_ to _A_, a selector vertex _s<sub>i</sub>_ to _B_, and two red edges _y<sub>i</sub>s<sub>i</sub>_ and _z<sub>i</sub>s<sub>i</sub>_. Finally, for \(i\in[n]\) we add blue edges between _y<sub>i</sub>_ and \(y_j^i\) for the values of _j_ for which \(x_i\in C_j\), and between _z<sub>i</sub>_ and \(z_j^i\) for the values of _j_ for which \(\overline{x_i}\in C_j\).

We claim that \(\Phi\) has a satisfying assignment if and only if _G_ admits a matching _M_ consisting of red edges whose end vertices cover every blue edge. Suppose there exists a satisfying assignment for \(\Phi\). Then for each _i_, we add the red edge _y<sub>i</sub>s<sub>i</sub>_ to _M_ if _x<sub>i</sub>_ was true, otherwise the edge _z<sub>i</sub>s<sub>i</sub>_. For each clause _C<sub>j</sub>_, we pick a literal that is true and add two red edges from \(a'_i\) and \(a''_i\) to the vertices corresponding to the other two literals. This way each blue edge will be covered. Indeed, if a blue edge is not covered at its vertex in _A_, then it corresponds to a false literal. However, in such a case the edge is covered in one of the _K_<sub>2,3</sub>s.

For the other direction, let _M_ be a red matching that covers every blue edge. In every red _K_<sub>2,3</sub>, there is a blue edge from one of its vertices in _B_ that is not covered by edges of the _K_<sub>2,3</sub>, hence it has to be covered by an edge _y<sub>i</sub>s<sub>i</sub>_ or _z<sub>i</sub>s<sub>i</sub>_, and only one of these two edges can be in _M_. If we set the values of the variables such that _x<sub>i</sub>_ is true if and only if \(y_is_i\in M\), then we get a satisfying assignment.
